# Simulating lines, pools and crosses {#sec-simulating-crosses}



The Foundations part defined the quantities the book manages -- coancestry
(@sec-coancestry) and its partition over two pools (@sec-subdivided) -- the
response they are traded against (@sec-response), and the heterosis that pool
divergence is maintained for (@sec-heterosis). @sec-response drew its data
from `simulate_pools()` and @sec-heterosis from `simulate_lines()` and
`simulate_data()`, both without deriving them. This chapter builds the generator
step by step, with `simulate_lines()` and `simulate_data()`.

`simulate_pools()` uses the same Balding-Nichols pool frequencies, homozygous lines and A x B
factorial, but a different trait: `n_qtl` loci with independent effects plus
noise, where the traits built here have correlated effects at every marker and
no noise. Up to the lines the two generators consume R's random stream in the
same order, so called with `book_cfg`'s values (25 +
25 lines, $m$ = 2000, `fst` = 0.15,
seed 1) they return the same lines and the same hybrid marker
matrix `X` (asserted in @sec-sim-lines); only the traits differ.

The `book_cfg` values coincide
with the arguments written in @sec-response's chunk, which asserts that its
`fst` and seed equal `book_cfg`'s. `simulate_pools()` also clamps its pool frequencies to
$[10^{-6}, 1 - 10^{-6}]$ and `simulate_lines()` does not, so the pool
frequencies of the two functions agree to within $10^{-6}$ and not exactly;
at the arguments of @sec-sim-lines the lines are identical (asserted there).

Everything downstream of this chapter consumes three objects and knows nothing
about where they came from. That is deliberate: it is the seam at which a
simulation is swapped for real data, and it is the only place that has to change
when it is.

This chapter builds those objects. It also builds the candidate set the rest of
the book selects from, so the choices made here -- how divergent the pools are
(@sec-sim-divergence), how the index is constructed (@sec-sim-traits) --
determine what the later chapters have to work
with.

## What has to be produced

@tbl-stage1-contract lists the three objects, and the optional fourth.


::: {#tbl-stage1-contract .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='The stage-1 contract: the objects stage 1 hands to stage 2, with their shape (N hybrids, m markers, L lines) and the computations that need them. Stage 2 runs without `fL`; it loses only the pool decomposition.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Object    |Shape              |Content                                           |Needed for                             |
|:---------|:------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------|
|`X`       |N x m              |hybrid marker matrix, values in 0/0.5/1           |every frequency-based metric           |
|`f`       |N x N              |molecular coancestry of the hybrids               |every coancestry-based metric          |
|`hybrids` |N x (3 + n_traits) |hybrid id, the two parent lines, predicted traits |the index, and the line-usage vector   |
|`fL`      |L x L, optional    |coancestry BETWEEN LINES                          |only the heterotic-group decomposition |


:::
:::


## Simulating the lines {#sec-sim-lines}

Two heterotic pools are generated with a Balding-Nichols-type model. From
@balding1995 this chapter takes the name of the model and the idea of
expressing the divergence of a population from a common ancestral one in a
single parameter; the Beta densities of @eq-balding-nichols and the reading of
$F_{BN}$ given with it are this book's own specification for a biallelic locus,
implemented in `simulate_lines()`, and are not quoted from that paper; the book
attributes to @balding1995 no particular parameterisation. Ancestral allele frequencies $p^{*}_k$ are drawn uniform on
$[0.05, 0.95]$, then pool A's frequency at marker $k$ is drawn as

$$p_{Ak} \sim \text{Beta}\!\left(p^{*}_k \frac{1 - F_{BN}}{F_{BN}},\;
                                (1 - p^{*}_k) \frac{1 - F_{BN}}{F_{BN}}\right),$$ {#eq-balding-nichols}

and independently for pool B ($p_{Bk}$), where $k = 1, \dots, m$ indexes
markers, $p^{*}_k \in [0.05, 0.95]$ is the ancestral frequency of the allele
coded 1, $p_{Ak}, p_{Bk} \in (0, 1)$ are the pool frequencies of that allele,
and $F_{BN} \in (0, 1)$ is the parameter `fst` of the configuration
(@sec-notation). The Beta of @eq-balding-nichols has mean $p^{*}_k$ and variance
$F_{BN}\, p^{*}_k (1 - p^{*}_k)$ (from $\mathrm{Var} = ab/[(a+b)^2(a+b+1)]$
with $a + b = (1 - F_{BN})/F_{BN}$): $F_{BN}$ is the divergence of *each* pool from
the ancestral frequency, measured as that variance in units of
$p^{*}_k(1 - p^{*}_k)$, not a divergence between the two pools. The ancestral
frequency $p^{*}_k$ belongs to the draw: it is a parameter of the simulation
and is never observed in the data. It is neither a pool frequency
$p_{Ak}$, $p_{Bk}$ nor the frozen base `ctx$p0` of the candidate set, which is
a sample quantity of the hybrids (defined at the end of @sec-ctx-built). Between the pools,
$\mathrm{Var}(p_{Ak} - p_{Bk}) = 2 F_{BN}\, p^{*}_k (1 - p^{*}_k)$, and the
$F_{ST}$ statistic of @eq-f-stats computed on two pools of unbounded size
estimates approximately $F_{BN}/(2 - F_{BN})$ (@sec-notation): at the book's
$F_{BN}$ = 0.15 that is 0.081,
not 0.15.

Genotypes are then drawn as $2 \times \text{Bernoulli}(p)$, which makes every
line fully homozygous, as an inbred line should be. @tbl-line-genotypes checks
the result.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
cat(deparse(simulate_lines), sep = "\n")

#>     p_anc <- stats::runif(cfg$m, 0.05, 0.95)
#>     bn <- function(p, fst) {
#>         stats::rbeta(length(p), p * (1 - fst)/fst, (1 - p) * 
#>             (1 - fst)/fst)
#>     }
#>     pA <- bn(p_anc, cfg$fst)
#>     pB <- bn(p_anc, cfg$fst)
#>     draw <- function(n, p) {
#>         matrix(2L * stats::rbinom(n * length(p), 1, rep(p, each = n)), 
#>             nrow = n)
#>     }
#>     L <- rbind(draw(cfg$n_pool_A, pA), draw(cfg$n_pool_B, pB))
#>     storage.mode(L) <- "double"
#>     L

```
:::

Only 0 and 2 appear: no residual heterozygotes. With real data those must be
imputed or dropped before this point, because the hybrid-genotype identity in
@sec-coancestry assumes homozygous parents.

### What the generator assumes {#sec-sim-assumptions}

The data of this chapter are generated under the assumptions listed here, and the
numbers it reports (the grid, the replicates, the expectations derived for the
divergence knob) are conditional on them. The exact algebraic identities it
checks do not need them all: the per-hybrid heterozygous fraction equals
$1 - f^L_{ab}$ for any inbred parents, the identity of $f$ with
`tcrossprod(cbind(X, 1 - X)) / m` holds for any marker matrix coded 0, 0.5, 1,
and $\sum G = 0$ holds for any panel centred on its own sample frequencies.
Independence across loci enters the dispersion of the replicates, not the
expectations, which are sums over loci.

- *Biallelic, neutral, unlinked markers.* The pools diverge by drift alone from
  one ancestral frequency vector (no selection, mutation or migration after the
  split), and the loci are independent of one another: $p^{*}_k$, $p_{Ak}$,
  $p_{Bk}$ and every genotype are drawn independently across $k$. There is no
  genetic map and no recombination, so no linkage disequilibrium arises beyond
  sampling noise. @sec-alphasimr relaxes this (linkage, outbred founders,
  directional dominance and several generations of selection).
- *Unrelated lines, inbred by fiat.* Given $p_{Ak}$, the lines of pool A are
  independent draws of $2 \times \text{Bernoulli}(p_{Ak})$ at each locus, and
  likewise for pool B: there is no pedigree and no shared descent among lines of
  a pool beyond what the pool frequency carries. Each line is drawn directly
  at fixation (0 or 2 at every marker); the generator does not model the
  doubled-haploid or selfing path that produces inbred lines in a programme
  (@sec-hp-cycle).
- *Equal pool sizes and the complete A x B factorial.* $n_A = n_B$ in the
  configuration, and every A x B combination is formed once, with equal weight
  (@sec-sim-hybrids). This is an assumption, not a property of hybrid programmes:
  the identities of the grid of @tbl-divergence-grid that tie the heterozygous fraction to
  $GD_T + GD_{BS}$ need it. @sec-mating and @sec-joint choose which crosses
  are made instead.
- *Additive traits, effects at every marker, known without error* (section
  "Predicted traits"): no dominance and no prediction error. Dominance enters in
  @sec-heterosis and @sec-alphasimr, and prediction error in
  @sec-genomic-prediction.

### The divergence knob {#sec-sim-divergence}

`fst` sets how much of the pools' diversity sits *between* them rather than
within; it is not compared here with the number of markers, the number of lines
or the trait correlation, so nothing is claimed about its rank among the
parameters. What the divergence buys is less obvious than it looks:
@fig-divergence-het plots the
heterozygous fraction of the F1 over a grid of $F_{BN}$,
@tbl-divergence-grid gives the coancestries and diversity components behind it,
and @tbl-divergence-trade the changes between the two ends of the grid. The
grid uses the teaching configuration (25 + 25
lines, $m$ = 2000) with `fst` replaced by the grid value, so its row at
$F_{BN}$ = 0.15 is the F1 of the lines `L` of @sec-sim-lines and the heterozygous
fraction of @tbl-diagonal of @sec-coancestry (asserted against `L` in the chunk).




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# the two trade ratios and the heterozygous fraction over replicate grids at the
# two ends; simulate_lines() seeds from cfg$seed, so seed s is explicit
gd_ends <- function(fst, seed) {
  cfg <- modifyList(book_cfg, list(fst = fst, seed = seed))
  fL  <- molecular_coancestry(simulate_lines(cfg) / 2)
  A <- seq_len(cfg$n_pool_A); B <- cfg$n_pool_A + seq_len(cfg$n_pool_B)
  f_til <- mean(c(fL[A, A], fL[B, B])); f_bar <- mean(fL)
  c(GD_WS = 1 - f_til, GD_BS = f_til - f_bar, GD_T = 1 - f_bar,
    het = 1 - mean(fL[A, B]))
}
n_rep <- 200
rep_lo <- vapply(seq_len(n_rep), function(s) gd_ends(min(fst_grid), s), numeric(4))
rep_hi <- vapply(seq_len(n_rep), function(s) gd_ends(max(fst_grid), s), numeric(4))
rep_x  <- rep_hi - rep_lo                        # change, largest minus smallest
rep_ratio <- rbind(-rep_x["GD_BS", ] / rep_x["GD_T", ],
                   -rep_x["GD_WS", ] / rep_x["GD_BS", ])
rep_het_diff <- rep_x["het", ]                   # paired by seed
```
:::





::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
d <- data.frame(fst = fst_grid, t(div))
# equal pool sizes: 1 - mean f^L_AB = GD_T + GD_BS exactly
dev_grid <- rel_dev(d$het_fraction, d$GD_T + d$GD_BS)
# the row at book_cfg$fst is the F1 of the lines L of this chapter
i_cfg <- which(d$fst == book_cfg$fst)
a_L <- seq_len(book_cfg$n_pool_A); b_L <- book_cfg$n_pool_A + seq_len(book_cfg$n_pool_B)
dev_row <- abs(d$het_fraction[i_cfg] -
               (1 - mean(molecular_coancestry(L / 2)[a_L, b_L])))
stopifnot(dev_grid < tol_exact, length(i_cfg) == 1, dev_row < tol_exact)
# replicate mean +/- s.d. at the two ends (rep_lo, rep_hi of the chunk above)

plot(d$fst, d$het_fraction, type = "b", pch = 19,
     ylim = y_rng + c(-1, 1) * 0.25 * diff(y_rng),
     xlab = expression(F[BN]),
     ylab = "heterozygous fraction of the F1")
abline(h = het_exp, lty = 2)
arrows(x_end, m_end - s_end, x_end, m_end + s_end, angle = 90, code = 3,
       length = 0.05, col = "grey35")
points(x_end, m_end, pch = 22, bg = "white", col = "grey35")
grid()
legend("bottomright", bty = "n", lty = c(1, NA, 2), pch = c(19, 22, NA),

```

Across a 20-fold range of $F_{BN}$ the
heterozygous fraction stays between 0.3617 and
0.3663, against an expectation of
0.3650 that contains no $F_{BN}$. Each point is one draw of a
finite pair of pools. Over 200 replicate draws (seeds 1 to 200, the
two ends of the grid only) the heterozygous fraction has mean
0.3651 (s.d. 0.0033) at
$F_{BN}$ = 0.02 and 0.3651 (s.d.
0.0059) at $F_{BN}$ = 0.40; the mean change
between the ends, paired by seed, is $2.2 \times 10^{-6}$ with standard
error $4.0 \times 10^{-4}$, 0.01
standard errors from zero. A single draw per point therefore
scatters by about 0.006, and
the range of the six single draws (0.0046) is of that
order: the figure by itself cannot separate a flat line from a small trend, and
the replicate means and the expectation of @sec-heterosis-flat are what carry the flatness.
Over the same range, in the terms of @sec-subdivided with $\tilde f$ the
group coancestry within a pool (self-coancestry included, `within_pool_f`),
the within-subpopulation gene diversity $GD_{WS} = 1 - \tilde f = GD_{WI} + GD_{BI}$ of @eq-gd-partition changes by $-$0.1323, the between-pool component $GD_{BS}$ by
0.0674 and the total $GD_T$ by $-$0.0649.

The $GD_{BS}$ gain is
1.04 times the $GD_T$ loss and the within-pool loss is
1.96 times the $GD_{BS}$ gain; the expectations under drift
in two equal pools are 1 and 2 (@sec-subdivided). Both ratios are single draws.
Over the 200 replicate grids they have mean 1.005 and
2.003 with standard deviation
0.086 and 0.086, so the
departure of this draw from 1 and 2 is within ordinary sampling variation.

The `stopifnot()` in the code of @fig-divergence-het
asserts the identity that ties the first trade to the flat line (deviation
$1.1 \times 10^{-16}$, tolerance $1 \times 10^{-12}$): with equal pool sizes the
heterozygous fraction is exactly $GD_T + GD_{BS}$, so a constant heterozygous
fraction means that what $GD_{BS}$ gains, $GD_T$ loses.

That is not an artefact of this grid, under the assumptions of @sec-sim-assumptions. For
the F1 of inbred parents $a$ and $b$ the heterozygous fraction is exactly
$1 - f^{L}_{ab}$, hybrid by hybrid (asserted in the chunk of
@tbl-ctx-check); its mean over the complete A x B factorial is
$1 - \bar f^{L}_{AB}$, with $\bar f^{L}_{AB}$ (`between_pool_f`) the mean
coancestry between a pool-A and a pool-B line (written $f_{AB}$ in
@sec-subdivided and $\theta_{AB}$ in @sec-notation; @sec-heterosis identifies
them on the complete factorial). @sec-heterosis-flat
derives the expectations for pools of unbounded size: the shared term
$2\bar p(1 - \bar p)$, which is $GD_T$ here, loses $F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})$
and the divergence term, which is $GD_{BS}$, gains the same amount. Here
$GD_T$ and $GD_{BS}$ are computed from the sample frequencies of $n$ lines per
pool, which add binomial variance $p_{Ak}(1 - p_{Ak})/n$ to each pool frequency;
then $E[GD_{BS}] = F_{BN}\,p^{*}q^{*} + (1 - F_{BN})\,p^{*}q^{*}/n$ per marker,
with $q^{*} = 1 - p^{*}$, and the loss of $GD_T$ and the gain of $GD_{BS}$
are both $F_{BN}\,p^{*}q^{*}(1 - 1/n)$ in expectation. The factor $(1 - 1/n)$
cancels in the ratios 1 and 2. With $n$ = 25 and the
$F_{BN}$ range of the grid, the expected change is
0.0666,
against 0.0693 for unbounded pools.
@sec-heterosis-flat derives the same expectation and the same sample-frequency
offset on a different grid (seed 5, $m$ = 2000); the formulas agree,
and the numbers here are a different draw of the generator.

What this chapter measures is the heterozygous fraction and its split into
$GD_T$ and $GD_{BS}$. Its data carry no dominance (the traits of @sec-sim-traits are
additive), so the heterozygous fraction is not heterosis here. It is the F1
heterosis per locus only for flat dominance, $d_k = 1$ at every locus
(@eq-het-value), and its identification with $GD_T + GD_{BS}$ needs in
addition inbred parents, the complete A x B factorial and equal pool weights,
the conditions of the $GD_{BS}$ row of @tbl-keystone. Under those conditions
neutral divergence relocates diversity from $GD_T$ to $GD_{BS}$ and creates no
expected heterosis. Outside them this chapter says nothing about heterosis. Whether $GD_{BS}$ is to be preserved is
not a consequence of the flat line: @tbl-keystone in @sec-subdivided states it
for those conditions and defers the argument to @sec-heterosis, and
@sec-heterosis-alignment treats what has to be true of the divergence, namely
its alignment with the dominance effects, for the divergence to be worth
anything.

## From lines to hybrids {#sec-sim-hybrids}

Every A x B combination is formed. With 25 lines per pool
that is 625 candidates; at the production
scale of 71 lines per pool it is 5041. @tbl-hybrid-dims gives the
size of the resulting dosage matrix `M` and @tbl-ped-head the first rows of the
pedigree `ped`.


::: {#tbl-hybrid-dims .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Dimensions of the hybrid dosage matrix `M` (values 0/1/2) at the teaching scale: one row per A x B combination, one column per marker.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
cfg <- book_cfg
a_ids <- seq_len(cfg$n_pool_A)
b_ids <- cfg$n_pool_A + seq_len(cfg$n_pool_B)
ped <- expand.grid(a = a_ids, b = b_ids)
M   <- (L[ped$a, , drop = FALSE] + L[ped$b, , drop = FALSE]) / 2   # 0/1/2
data.frame(dimension = c("hybrids (rows of M)", "markers (columns of M)"),
           value = dim(M))
```

The factorial structure matters more than it looks. Because every line appears
in many candidate hybrids, selecting hybrids is really selecting *line usage* --
and that observation, made precise in @sec-collapse, is what makes the whole
problem tractable at production scale.

## Predicted traits {#sec-sim-traits}

Marker effects are drawn correlated across traits, through a Cholesky factor of
a fixed correlation matrix, and the predicted values are the centered marker
matrix times those effects. In this chapter `R` (the target correlation of the
marker effects), `B` (the matrix of marker effects) and `L` (the line genotype
matrix) are names of code objects, not the $\mathbf R$, $\mathbf B$ and $L$ of
@sec-notation, and $n_A$, $n_B$ count the lines of pool A and pool B, not the
female and male lines of @sec-mating.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(cfg$seed + 99)
R <- matrix(c(1, 0.3, -0.3,
              0.3, 1,  0.1,
             -0.3, 0.1, 1), 3, 3)
stopifnot(nrow(R) == cfg$n_traits)       # R is written for three traits
vr <- vanraden_G(M)
B <- matrix(rnorm(cfg$m * cfg$n_traits), cfg$m) %*% chol(R)
traits <- scale(vr$Z %*% B)
rank_Z <- qr(vr$Z)$rank
stopifnot(rank_Z == cfg$n_pool_A + cfg$n_pool_B - 2)
```
:::


@tbl-trait-cor sets the realised correlations of the predicted traits beside
the target `R`.


::: {#tbl-trait-cor .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Target correlation `R` of the marker effects and realised correlation of the predicted traits over the hybrids, for each pair of traits; one draw of marker effects at the teaching scale.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
ij <- which(upper.tri(R), arr.ind = TRUE)
fmt(data.frame(traits = paste(ij[, 1], "x", ij[, 2]),
               target_R = R[ij], realised = cor(traits)[ij]), 3)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}

|traits | target_R| realised|
|:------|--------:|--------:|
|1 x 2  |      0.3|    0.259|
|1 x 3  |     -0.3|   -0.440|
|2 x 3  |      0.1|    0.049|

:::
:::


The Cholesky step gives each row of `B`, the effects of one marker on the
3 traits, covariance `R`. It does not make the realised trait
correlations equal `R`: they depart from it by up to
0.140 in absolute value. The hybrid values are
linear combinations of the columns of the centred matrix `Z`, whose rank is
48 $= (n_A - 1) + (n_B - 1)$ for an additive A x B factorial, so each
realised correlation rests on one draw of effects projected onto 48
dimensions. The target is a property of the effect distribution, not of this
draw; how closely the realised correlations approach it on average over draws
was not measured here.

::: {.callout-important}
## What this simulation deliberately does not model

These predicted values are constructed from *known* marker effects, so they
carry no prediction error. Real genomic estimated breeding values (GEBVs) do.
The book therefore treats `ctx$index` as given throughout.

- *The optimum.* For a given candidate set and a given constraint on diversity,
  no selection made on estimated values can have a higher mean true index than
  the optimum computed on the known values, because the optimum maximises that
  index over every feasible selection. This is a statement about the optimum.
- *The heuristics.* The gains this book reports come from greedy,
  differential-evolution and local-search selections, which at book scale are
  not certified optima (@sec-bound; `ocs_bound()` gives a valid upper bound, and
  `sel_exact()` does not converge there). A feasible selection is not a bound: a
  selection made on estimates could exceed a heuristic's index on the known
  values, so a gain in `ctx$index` does not bound the gain that a selection on
  estimates could achieve.
- *Scope.* That statement about the optimum concerns the index only: it does
  not apply to the diversity metrics, which do not depend on the traits, nor to
  anything outside the additive model.
- *Additive only.* The additive model also carries no dominance, so it cannot
  express specific combining ability (@sec-heterosis-gca-sca models it; the
  caveats of @sec-case-study remain); the gap in prediction is closed in
  @sec-genomic-prediction.
:::

## The two matrices, both built {#sec-ctx-built}


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
X <- M / 2
ctx <- build_ctx(X = X, f = molecular_coancestry(X), G = vr$G, traits = traits,
                 ped = ped, n_lines = nrow(L),
                 pool = rep(c("A", "B"), c(cfg$n_pool_A, cfg$n_pool_B)),
                 fL = molecular_coancestry(L / 2), cfg = cfg)

# the heterozygous fraction of hybrid (a, b) is 1 - fL[a, b] (inbred parents)
dev_G   <- abs(sum(ctx[["G"]])) / sum(abs(ctx[["G"]]))   # relative to sum |G|
dev_f   <- rel_dev(ctx[["f"]], tcrossprod(cbind(X, 1 - X)) / ncol(X))
dev_het <- rel_dev(rowMeans(ctx[["X"]] == 0.5),
                   1 - ctx[["fL"]][cbind(ped$a, ped$b)])
stopifnot(dev_G < tol_exact,
          min(ctx[["f"]]) >= 0, max(ctx[["f"]]) <= 1,
          dev_f < tol_exact, dev_het < tol_exact)

# simulate_data() builds the same ctx, apart from the column names of traits
ctx_sd <- simulate_data(book_cfg)
same <- setdiff(names(ctx), "traits")
stopifnot(identical(names(ctx_sd), names(ctx)),
          all(vapply(same, function(k)
            isTRUE(all.equal(ctx[[k]], ctx_sd[[k]], tolerance = tol_exact)),
            logical(1))),
          isTRUE(all.equal(unname(ctx[["traits"]]), unname(ctx_sd[["traits"]]),
                           tolerance = tol_exact, check.attributes = FALSE)))
```
:::





::: {#tbl-ctx-check .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Size of the context `ctx` built in this chapter (N hybrids, m markers, number of lines) and the two properties checked on its matrices: the sum of the elements of VanRaden\'s G, printed in scientific notation because it is zero only up to rounding, and the range of the molecular coancestry f. The code asserts $|\mathrm{sum}(G)| / \sum |G|$ < $1 \times 10^{-12}$.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  quantity = c("N", "m", "n_lines", "sum(G)", "min(f)", "max(f)"),
  value = c(sprintf("%d", c(ctx[["N"]], ctx[["m"]], ctx[["n_lines"]])),
            fmt_sci(sum(ctx[["G"]]), 3),
            sprintf("%.4f", c(min(ctx[["f"]]), max(ctx[["f"]]))))),
  align = c("l", "r"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|quantity |                   value|
|:--------|-----------------------:|
|N        |                     625|
|m        |                    2000|
|n_lines  |                      50|
|sum(G)   | $-4.18 \times 10^{-11}$|
|min(f)   |                  0.6448|
|max(f)   |                  0.8317|


:::
:::


@tbl-ctx-check shows the result. `sum(G)` is zero up to floating-point
rounding: it is $-4.18 \times 10^{-11}$, $1.5 \times 10^{-15}$ of
$\sum |G|$, and not exactly 0. It is zero because `vanraden_G()` centres the markers
on the sample frequencies of this very panel, `colMeans(M) / 2`, so that the
columns of $\mathbf Z$ sum to zero and $\mathbf 1'\mathbf G\mathbf 1 = 0$
(@eq-g-sum-zero); `G` here is the matrix of @eq-vanraden-g [@vanraden2008],
and the property belongs to this centring, not to the matrix at other
reference frequencies, where the sum need not vanish. `f` is inside $[0, 1]$,
the other property of @sec-coancestry, on this dataset. Two identities are
asserted with it (tolerance $1 \times 10^{-12}$): `f` equals
`tcrossprod(cbind(X, 1 - X)) / m` to exactly 0, and the heterozygous
fraction of each hybrid equals `1 - fL[a, b]` to $5.6 \times 10^{-17}$. The range
of `f` is nonetheless narrow and far from 0: `f` is identity in state, unrelated individuals are not
at 0 and its level is set by the marker panel (@sec-coancestry), so the
assertion `min(f) >= 0` is the weak property and the informative one is the
range printed in the table.

The context also stores three objects computed once, from the 625
hybrids, at construction, and not to be recomputed per scenario (@tbl-ctx-stored):


::: {#tbl-ctx-stored .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='The three objects stored once in `ctx` at construction: number of values (`p0` and `maf_pop` one per marker, `index` one per hybrid) and their range.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
stored <- ctx[c("p0", "maf_pop", "index")]
fmt(data.frame(object = names(stored),
               n_values = vapply(stored, length, integer(1)),
               min = vapply(stored, min, numeric(1)),
               max = vapply(stored, max, numeric(1)),
               row.names = NULL))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}

|object  | n_values|     min|    max|
|:-------|--------:|-------:|------:|
|p0      |     2000|  0.0000| 1.0000|
|maf_pop |     2000|  0.0000| 0.5000|
|index   |      625| -2.4068| 3.6491|

:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# p0 is the mean of the two pools' sampled line frequencies (L is coded 0/2)
dev_p0 <- rel_dev(ctx[["p0"]], (colMeans(L[a_ids, ]) + colMeans(L[b_ids, ])) / 4)
stopifnot(dev_p0 < tol_exact)
```
:::


`p0` is the allele frequency vector of the candidate set, `colMeans(X)` over the
625 hybrids. It is the **base** against which `F_hom` and `F_drift`
are measured in @sec-genomic-era, and recomputing it per scenario would
silently zero out the historical memory of erosion. It is a sample quantity of
this draw: with equal pools and the complete factorial it is the mean of the
two pools' sampled line frequencies (asserted in the chunk of @tbl-ctx-stored, deviation $1.1 \times 10^{-16}$). It is therefore a different object from the
ancestral frequency $p^{*}_k$ of @eq-balding-nichols, which is never observed,
and from the pool frequencies $p_{Ak}$, $p_{Bk}$. `maf_pop` is the minor-allele
frequency of `p0`, `pmin(p0, 1 - p0)`, and `index` is the multi-trait index of
the hybrids, standardised once.

For real data the same function is called with your own matrices:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
st1 <- stage1_build(
  X      = hybrid_markers,   # N x m, coded 0/1/2 or 0/0.5/1
  ped    = pedigree,         # data.frame with columns a, b
  traits = predicted_traits, # N x n_traits
  fL     = line_coancestry,  # optional
  coding = "012"             # or "0-0.5-1"; NULL (default) auto-detects
)
```
:::


`stage1_build()` rescales 0/1/2 dosages to 0/0.5/1 before computing `f`. With
`coding = NULL` it infers the coding from the values present, ignoring missing
calls: any value above 1 means 0/1/2. That rule assumes a 0/1/2 matrix contains
at least one dosage-2 call. A matrix holding only 0 and 1 is ambiguous -- inbred
lines coded 0/0.5/1, or 0/1/2 dosages with no homozygote for the allele coded
2 -- and no rule applied to the values can resolve it; `stage1_build()` then
assumes 0/0.5/1 and warns. Declaring `coding` removes the assumption. On the
simulated hybrids, which contain dosage-2 calls, the two codings give the same
`f`:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
tr <- st1$hybrids[, grep("^trait", names(st1$hybrids))]
pd <- data.frame(a = st1$hybrids$line_A, b = st1$hybrids$line_B)
stopifnot(any(st1$X * 2 == 2),
          identical(stage1_build(st1$X, pd, tr)$f,
                    stage1_build(st1$X * 2, pd, tr)$f))
```
:::


The ambiguous case: two hybrids at three markers, coded 0/1/2, with no
dosage-2 call. Auto-detection reads each 1 as a homozygote, so it returns the
coancestry of two inbred individuals that these hybrids are not; the declared coding returns the
coancestry computed directly from the 0/0.5/1 matrix (@tbl-coding-ambiguous).


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
X_amb   <- rbind(c(0, 1, 1),
                 c(1, 0, 1))                 # 0/1/2 dosages, no dosage 2
ped_amb <- data.frame(a = 1:2, b = 3:4)
tr_amb  <- data.frame(trait1 = c(0, 0))
f_auto <- withCallingHandlers(
  stage1_build(X_amb, ped_amb, tr_amb)$f,
  warning = function(w) { message("warning: ", conditionMessage(w))
                          invokeRestart("muffleWarning") })
f_012  <- stage1_build(X_amb, ped_amb, tr_amb, coding = "012")$f
f_true <- molecular_coancestry(X_amb / 2)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(f_012, f_true)),
          !isTRUE(all.equal(f_auto, f_true)))
```
:::



::: {#tbl-coding-ambiguous .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Molecular coancestry of the two hybrids of the ambiguous example (`f11`, `f22`: self-coancestries; `f12`: between them) as returned by `stage1_build()` with the coding auto-detected and with `coding = "012"` declared, and as computed directly by `molecular_coancestry()` on the matrix divided by 2.'}

```{.r .cell-code}

  coding = c("auto-detected", "declared 012", "direct, X / 2"),
  f11 = c(f_auto[1, 1], f_012[1, 1], f_true[1, 1]),
  f22 = c(f_auto[2, 2], f_012[2, 2], f_true[2, 2]),
  f12 = c(f_auto[1, 2], f_012[1, 2], f_true[1, 2])))
```

## What the candidate set looks like

@fig-candidate-pool shows the two quantities every later chapter trades: the
index of the candidates and the gene diversity of random subsets of them.




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 2.5, 1))
hist(ctx$index, breaks = 40, col = "grey85", border = "white",
     main = "multi-trait index", xlab = "index (s.d. units)")
set.seed(cfg$seed + 3)
gd_random <- replicate(n_subsets, gene_diversity(sample.int(ctx$N, n_sub), ctx))
hist(gd_random, breaks = 30, col = "grey85", border = "white",
     main = paste("GD of random subsets of", n_sub), xlab = "gene diversity")
abline(v = gene_diversity(seq_len(ctx$N), ctx), col = book_pal[["ink"]], lwd = 2)
par(op)
```

The dark vertical line is the gene diversity of the *whole* candidate set. It does not sit at the
centre of the distribution of random subsets of 60 -- it sits above it. That gap
is pure sampling, it has nothing to do with selection, and mistaking it for a
loss is the subject of @sec-baseline. @tbl-gd-baseline gives the size of the
gap, from one set of 400 random subsets, with the Monte Carlo
standard error of their mean: the gap is 59 standard errors, so it is
not sampling noise of the subsets. @sec-baseline measures the same gap on the same `ctx` with its own subsets and
derives its expectation, and the percentages differ only by the draw of the
subsets.
